title: Capstone Project - Part 1: Design and Build
summary: The capstone ties everything together. Today you choose a meaningful problem, design a clean architecture combining RAG and/or agents, and implement the core functionality with a proper project structure. A strong capstone is the centerpiece of a Gen
content:
# Capstone Project - Part 1: Design and Build ##### The chatbot that nobody needed A student in Nagpur spent five weeks on his capstone: a chatbot that answered questions about the Bhagavad Gita using RAG. Technically clean — good chunking, a reranker, citations, a Streamlit UI, deployed on Hugging Face Spaces. At the review, a mentor asked: *"Who uses this?"* He did not have an answer. He had built it because RAG over a text corpus was the tutorial he had followed, and the Gita was a text corpus he had access to. There was no user, no problem, and no reason for the thing to exist. Meanwhile a classmate had built something much simpler — a WhatsApp bot that answered questions about a specific government scholarship scheme, in Hindi and Marathi, from the official PDF guidelines. Cruder retrieval, no reranker, plain prompt. But 340 real users in its first month, mostly students in tier-3 towns who could not parse a 60-page English PDF. Guess which one got interview callbacks. **A capstone is judged on whether it solves a problem, not on how many techniques it uses.** Today is about choosing well and building the core properly. Part 2 finishes it. ##### Choosing a problem The best capstone problems share four properties: - **A real user you can name.** Not "students" — *"final-year students in Nagpur applying for the post-matric scholarship."* - **A problem you have observed**, ideally one you or someone you know has hit. - **Data you can actually get.** Public documents, your college's records, an open API, a corpus you can scrape legally. - **Scoped to two weeks.** Not "an AI tutor for all subjects" but "a doubt-solver for one Class 12 physics textbook." **Good capstone patterns**, in rough order of how often they work well: | Pattern | Example | Uses | |---|---|---| | **Domain RAG assistant** | Scholarship scheme Q&A in Hindi | Days 33–36 | | **Document processing** | Invoice extraction to structured JSON | Days 26, 39 | | **Agentic research tool** | Market research with search + synthesis | Day 37 | | **Multimodal assistant** | Damage assessment from photos | Day 39 | | **Fine-tuned specialist** | Support replies in a brand voice | Days 28–29 | **Anti-patterns to avoid:** a generic ChatGPT clone, "chat with any PDF" with no specific domain, anything requiring data you do not have, and anything so broad you cannot evaluate whether it works. **A useful test:** can you write, in one sentence, what someone can do with your system that they could not do before? If not, reconsider the problem before you write code. ##### The project spec One page, written before any code. This is your practical task, and it takes ninety minutes. ```markdown # ScholarshipBot — Project Spec ## Problem Maharashtra's post-matric scholarship guidelines are a 62-page English PDF. Students in tier-3 towns, often more comfortable in Marathi or Hindi, cannot determine eligibility or required documents without help. College offices field the same 20 questions hundreds of times each admission season. ## Users Final-year students applying for the scheme; college scholarship-cell staff. ## What it does Answers eligibility, document, and deadline questions in English, Hindi, or Marathi, citing the exact clause and page from the official PDF. ## Out of scope (v1) - Submitting applications - Personalised eligibility verdicts (legal risk — we surface criteria only) - Schemes other than post-matric Maharashtra ## Success criteria - Answers 20 benchmark questions correctly with correct citations (>= 85%) - Refuses cleanly when the answer is not in the document (100% on 5 probes) - p95 latency < 6s - Works in all three languages ## Architecture [diagram] ## Tech stack Ingestion: PyPDFLoader + RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter Embeddings: intfloat/multilingual-e5-base (multilingual — required) Vector store: Chroma (persisted) Reranker: BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 LLM: gpt-4o-mini API: FastAPI | UI: Gradio | Deploy: HF Spaces (Docker) ## Risks - Multilingual retrieval quality — mitigate by embedding queries and chunks with the same multilingual model, and testing all three languages - PDF table extraction (income slabs are in tables) — extract separately - Hallucinated clause numbers — number-grounding check from Day 40 ``` **The "out of scope" section is the most valuable part.** It is what stops you adding features in week two instead of finishing. ##### Architecture design Draw it before you build it. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph ING["Ingestion — offline, run once"] A["Official PDF
62 pages"] --> B["PyPDFLoader
keep page numbers"] B --> C["Extract tables
separately"] B --> D["Recursive split
800 / 150 overlap"] C --> E["Prepend section
headings to chunks"] D --> E E --> F["Embed
multilingual-e5"] F --> G[("Chroma
+ metadata")] end subgraph QRY["Query — per request"] H["User question
en / hi / mr"] --> I["Guardrails:
injection + moderation"] I --> J["Hybrid retrieve
top-25"] G --> J J --> K["Rerank → top-5"] K --> L["Prompt: context +
cite + refuse rules"] L --> M["LLM"] M --> N["Number-grounding
check"] N --> O["Answer + clause citations"] end O --> P["Log: trace, cost,
feedback"] ``` **Design principles for a capstone:** - **Simplest thing that solves the problem.** Add the reranker because retrieval measurably needs it, not because Day 36 mentioned it. - **Every component justified in one sentence.** If you cannot say why it is there, remove it. - **Measurable at each stage.** You cannot improve what you cannot measure — and Part 2 will ask for numbers. - **Deployable from day one.** Do not leave containerisation to the end. ##### Repository structure ``` scholarshipbot/ ├── README.md # spec, architecture, setup, results ├── pyproject.toml # pinned dependencies ├── Makefile # make ingest / make serve / make eval ├── .env.example # variable names, no values ├── .gitignore # .env, data/, __pycache__, *.chroma ├── Dockerfile ├── docker-compose.yml │ ├── app/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── main.py # FastAPI │ ├── config.py # pydantic-settings │ ├── rag.py # retrieve → rerank → generate │ ├── prompts.py # versioned PromptVersion objects │ └── guardrails.py # injection, moderation, grounding checks │ ├── ingest/ │ ├── load.py # PDF → documents │ ├── chunk.py # splitting + heading enrichment │ └── build_index.py # embed and persist │ ├── ui/ │ └── app.py # Gradio │ ├── eval/ │ ├── testset.jsonl # 20 Q&A with expected citations │ └── run_eval.py # RAGAS + rule checks │ ├── tests/ │ ├── test_chunk.py │ └── test_guardrails.py │ └── data/ # gitignored ├── raw/ └── chroma/ ``` **Three structural rules that separate a project from a notebook:** 1. **Notebooks explore; modules ship.** Anything the app depends on lives in a `.py` file with a test. 2. **Configuration in one place.** No hardcoded paths, model names, or chunk sizes scattered through the code. 3. **Commit early and often.** A history of forty meaningful commits demonstrates iteration; one commit called "final" demonstrates nothing. ```makefile .PHONY: setup ingest serve ui eval test setup: python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]" ingest: python -m ingest.build_index --pdf data/raw/scheme.pdf --out data/chroma serve: uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 ui: python ui/app.py eval: python eval/run_eval.py --testset eval/testset.jsonl test: pytest tests/ -v ``` A `Makefile` means a reviewer runs `make setup && make ingest && make serve` and your project works. That is a real differentiator. ##### Building the ingestion pipeline ```python # ingest/chunk.py from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_core.documents import Document import re def enrich_and_split(pages: list[Document], chunk_size=800, overlap=150) -> list[Document]: """Split pages into chunks, prepending the section heading to each.""" splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=chunk_size, chunk_overlap=overlap, separators=["\n\n", "\n", "। ", ". ", " ", ""], # Devanagari danda first ) chunks: list[Document] = [] current_section = "Introduction" for page in pages: heading = re.search(r"^\s*(\d+\.\s+[A-Z][^\n]{5,80})\s*$", page.page_content, re.MULTILINE) if heading: current_section = heading.group(1).strip() for piece in splitter.split_documents([page]): piece.page_content = f"[{current_section}]\n\n{piece.page_content}" piece.metadata.update({ "section": current_section, "page": page.metadata.get("page", 0) + 1, # 1-indexed for humans "n_chars": len(piece.page_content), }) chunks.append(piece) return chunks ``` Note the Devanagari `।` in the separators — a small detail that matters enormously for Marathi and Hindi text, and one that a generic tutorial would not mention. **The domain-specific details are where a capstone shows real thought.** ```python # ingest/build_index.py import argparse from pathlib import Path import chromadb from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader from .chunk import enrich_and_split def build(pdf_path: str, out_dir: str, model="intfloat/multilingual-e5-base"): pages = PyPDFLoader(pdf_path).load() chunks = enrich_and_split(pages) print(f"{len(pages)} pages → {len(chunks)} chunks") client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=out_dir) collection = client.get_or_create_collection( name="scheme", embedding_function=embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction( model_name=model), metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}, ) stem = Path(pdf_path).stem collection.upsert( # upsert, so re-runs are idempotent ids=[f"{stem}::c{i}" for i in range(len(chunks))], documents=[f"passage: {c.page_content}" for c in chunks], # E5 prefix metadatas=[c.metadata for c in chunks], ) print(f"indexed {collection.count()} chunks → {out_dir}") if __name__ == "__main__": p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("--pdf", required=True) p.add_argument("--out", default="data/chroma") build(**vars(p.parse_args())) ``` Two details carried forward: `upsert` rather than `add` so re-ingestion is idempotent (Day 34), and the `"passage: "` prefix that E5 models expect (Day 33). **Then inspect your chunks.** Print twenty at random and read them. This five-minute check catches more problems than any amount of parameter tuning. ##### The generation core ```python # app/prompts.py from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(frozen=True) class PromptVersion: name: str; version: str; system: str; user_template: str model: str; temperature: float; notes: str = "" ANSWER_V2 = PromptVersion( name="scheme_answer", version="v2", model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.0, system=( "You answer questions about the Maharashtra post-matric scholarship " "scheme using ONLY the provided context.\n\n" "Rules:\n" "1. Answer in the SAME language as the question (English, Hindi, or Marathi).\n" "2. Cite the section and page for every claim: [Section, p.N].\n" "3. Quote exact figures, dates, and percentages from the context. Never estimate.\n" "4. If the context does not answer the question, reply exactly:\n" " 'This is not covered in the official guidelines. Please contact your " "college scholarship cell.'\n" "5. Never tell a user whether they personally qualify. State the criteria " "and let them judge.\n" "6. Be concise: 4 sentences maximum." ), user_template="Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}", notes="v2: added rule 5 after v1 gave eligibility verdicts (legal risk)", ) ``` **Rule 5 is the kind of thing that makes a capstone credible.** It shows you thought about consequences, not just correctness — and the `notes` field records *why* the rule exists, which is exactly the versioning discipline from Day 42. ##### Building order ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Spec + repo
scaffold"] --> B["2. Ingestion
+ inspect chunks"] B --> C["3. Eval set
20 questions"] C --> D["4. Naive retrieval
measure baseline"] D --> E["5. Generation
+ citations"] E --> F["6. Improve retrieval
measure each change"] F --> G["7. API + UI"] G --> H["Part 2:
guardrails, deploy,
monitor, document"] ``` **Write the evaluation set at step 3, before you optimise anything.** Twenty questions with expected answers and expected source pages. Without a baseline, every subsequent change is a guess — and with one, you can report "hybrid search took recall@5 from 0.68 to 0.84," which is the sentence that makes a reviewer take you seriously. ##### Common mistakes - **Building without a named user** — the Gita chatbot. - **Scope that grows weekly** instead of shipping v1. - **No evaluation set**, so you cannot show improvement. - **Everything in one notebook**, unrunnable by anyone else. - **Adding components because the course covered them** rather than because retrieval needed them. - **Leaving deployment to the last day** and discovering a dependency conflict. - **Hardcoded paths and API keys.** - **Not inspecting chunks**, then wondering why retrieval is poor. - **One commit at the end**, hiding all evidence of iteration. - **No "out of scope" section**, so nothing is ever finished. - **English-only assumptions** in a multilingual context — wrong splitter separators, wrong embedding model. ##### Hands-on: spec first, code second Your practical task is the one-page spec and repository scaffold. Resist starting with code. Write the problem, the named user, the success criteria with actual numbers, and the out-of-scope list. Draw the architecture in Mermaid so it lives in your README. Then scaffold the directory structure and the Makefile, make your first commit, and only then start building. The mini project builds the core: ingestion through generation, with citations working end to end. Follow the build order above and resist skipping step 3. Once your naive baseline is measured, every improvement becomes a number you can quote — and that progression table is the strongest thing in your final write-up. The assignment is the ingestion pipeline and generation logic, cleanly written and version-controlled. "Clean" means specific things here: functions under thirty lines, configuration in one place, at least two tests, docstrings on public functions, and commits that describe what changed. A reviewer who clones your repo should be running it within five minutes. ##### Key takeaways - **A capstone is judged on whether it solves a real problem for a nameable user** — technique count is not the metric, and the simpler project with 340 users beat the sophisticated one with none. - **Write the one-page spec before any code**, and treat the "out of scope" section as the thing that lets you finish. - **Build the evaluation set before you optimise**, so every improvement is a measured number rather than a feeling. - **Structure the repo so a stranger can run it**: modules not notebooks, a Makefile, pinned dependencies, and configuration in one place. - **Domain-specific details are where real thought shows** — the Devanagari separator, the E5 prefix, the rule against giving eligibility verdicts.
